article_text:
Veteran Iranian filmmaker Majid Majidi has won Best Film at the 31st Busan International Film Festival for “ Midday Meal ,” his simple, starkly powerful contemporary parable about a rural schoolteacher making difficult moral choices to ensure his students continue to receive a free lunch in the face of government cuts.

Majidi received the prize from this year’s Competition jury president, celebrated Chinese director Zhang Yimou , and proceeded to make an impassioned speech protesting the war in Iran — in particular decrying the Minab school attack in February this year, which saw 156 civilians (120 of them schoolchildren) killed by a U.S. military strike. “They will stand firm to the end and fight to get their independence back,” Majidi said, before concluding: “I wish for a future with no war.”

With its humanist approach to social realism and its particular focus on child welfare, “Midday Meal” is of a piece with Majidi’s oeuvre, which includes such films as “The Color of Paradise” and the 2020 Venice competition entry “Sun Children”; he remains best known internationally for his 1998 film “Children of Heaven,” the first Iranian production ever to be nominated in the category today named Best International Feature. In an appreciative review of his latest, Variety critic Kambole Campbell wrote :”Majidi’s matter-of-fact style of shooting underlines the cold reality that [his protagonist] tries to navigate, and strips away any semblance of potential didacticism.”

Popular on Variety

“Midday Meal” could potentially return Majidi to Oscar contention: Under new Academy rules instated this year, the Busan win automatically qualifies the film for the Best International Feature Oscar, without any need for its home country to formally submit it for consideration. (Iran has already entered the lower-profile “Land of Angels” this year.) Busan is the sixth and final festival in the calendar to be granted this status; other films guaranteed eligibility by the new rule include festival prizewinners “Shame and Money” and “To Hold a Mountain” (both Sundance), “Yellow Letters” (Berlin), “Fjord” (Cannes), “Woman Unknown” (Cannes) and “Angh” (Toronto).

Other winners in Busan’s main competition — programmed entirely with films from Asian nations, most of them world premieres — include the Taiwanese family drama “ To Be Ordinary ,” which took Best Director for Lee Yun Chan, whose helming was commended in Variety’s review for its “handsome sobriety” and “delicate, empathetic touch.” It’s the first feature in over 15 years from Lee, who noted in her speech that she was wearing the same gown she wore when she premiered her 2005 debut “The Shoe Fairy” at Busan.

A Special Jury Prize went to Indonesian director Eddie Cahyono for his film “ Ibuku ,” about a working-class Indonesian widow struggling to stay afloat when her adult daughter lands in prison in Saudi Arabia, praised by Campbell as “most compelling when its spiritual qualities are felt rather than seen.”

The gender-neutral acting award was shared by two female performers: Japanese newcomer Kashun Himeno, whose performance as a lovestruck highschooler in the charmer “Satoko Always” was described by Variety critic James Marsh as “eye-catching [and] potentially star-making”; and Chinese star Zhou Xun as a single mother coping with her father’s death in director Gu You’s tearjerker “ The First Taste of Loneliness .” Gu’s film, praised by Variety as “patient, restrained and gracefully observed,” additionally took the Artistic Contribution Award for sound designer Danfeng Li.

In the separately juried New Currents competition for first features, Indian filmmaker Shashank Walia emerged as the winner for his film “Birds in the Dark,” about corruption and land disputes in rural Punjab; South Korean director Lim Ha-yeon’s “Beach Fictions,” a delightful, time-slipping romantic drama that also played in the main competition, received a special jury mention.

Zhang was joined on the formidable Competition jury by fellow Chinese filmmaker Bi Gan, as well as directors Kei Ishikawa and July Jung, actors Samal Yeslyamova and Choi Hee-seo, and producer Tran Thi Bich Ngoc, all of whom acted as presenters at the flashy outdoor closing ceremony at the ultra-modern Busan Film Center, with South Korean singer-actor Yim Si-wan (“Squid Game”) serving as master of ceremonies.

A surfeit of other prizes were handed out at yesterday’s Busan Vision Awards ceremony, where Mongolian-German production “Zogsool” took a quartet of prizes, while Spanish Oscar hopeful “La Bola Negra” added yet another festival audience award to its roster. More on those here .

Art Movements

Documenta 16 Names Four New Curatorial Team Members

The embattled German exhibition's latest appointments, artist Catherine Opie wins a Yale University award, and Dallas Art Fair partners with … a university?

Art Movements, published every Thursday afternoon, is a roundup of must-know news, appointments, awards, and other happenings in today’s chaotic art world.

Documenta Appoints New Curatorial Team Members

Less than eight months away from the 16th edition of Documenta , the German contemporary arts festival has appointed four new curatorial team members: artist and musician Raven Chacon will serve as curator-at-Large, and Osei Bonsu , Timea Junghaus , and Noam Segal will be curatorial advisors.

The upcoming iteration, opening on June 12 in Kassel, promises to offer a space for “study, experimentation, and awakening, where artists hold right to expression alongside their artistic creation.” But artists and free speech advocates have argued that this stated mission jars with Documenta’s adoption of a controversial definition of antisemitism that includes criticism of Israel, raising serious questions about creative freedom . In a recent interview with the German newspaper Die Zeit , Artistic Director Naomi Beckwith revealed that some artists have already declined to participate in Documenta 16 over Germany's support of Israel's genocide in Gaza.

Chacon, Bonsu, Junghaus, and Segal will join Beckwith and the core curatorial team for the 16th edition — Carla Acevedo-Yates , Romi Crawford , Mayra A. Rodríguez Castro , and Xiaoyu Weng — to help shape the program's artistic vision.

Leider aber durchkreuzt der tollpatschige Bauer der „Mossy Bottom“-Farm ihre Pläne, als er in das Gemüsebeet stolpert und alle Kürbisse zerstört. Wie immer hat der pfiffige Shaun eine Idee, um das Fest noch zu retten: Als er mit Wachstumsmitteln experimentiert, erschafft er allerdings ein haariges Monstrum, das fortan Angst und Schrecken verbreiten wird.

Mit Referenzen auf Horrorklassiker

Die Filmgeschichte steckt voller verrückter Wissenschaftler, die mit waghalsigen Experimenten gerne auch mal ihre Umwelt gefährden. Der berühmteste der Filmgeschichte ist wohl Dr. Frankenstein, basierend auf Mary Shelleys berühmtem Schauerroman , der unbedingt neues Leben erschaffen möchte. Auf die düstere Geschichte wurde schon dutzende Male referiert. Und auch das dritte Kino-Abenteuer der „Shaun das Schaf“-Filmreihe bedient sich nun munter daran.

Bei den Kürbis-Experimenten verwandelt sich Shaun, einst in einem „ Wallace & Gromit “-Film von Nick Park eingeführt, in einen waschechten verrückten Wissenschaftler – inklusive wolliger Sturmfrisur und einem diabolischen Gelächter. Wie so oft bei den Filmen der Stop-Motion-Schmiede Aardman Animations wird munter aus dem Fundus legendärer Filmklassiker zitiert: Neben „ Frankenstein “ sind es diesmal auch weitere Horrorklassiker wie „ Psycho “ oder „ Godzilla “.

So zündet auch der dritte Kinofilm – nach „ Shaun das Schaf - Der Film “ und „ Shaun das Schaf - Der Film: UFO-Alarm “ – „ein Feuerwerk an witzigen Einfällen, liebevoll gezeichneten Figuren und kulturgeschichtlichen Referenzen“, wie es in der Filmdienst-Kritik von Katharina Zeckau heißt. Wieder geht es um Freundschaft und Solidarität zwischen Shaun, der Schafsherde, Wachhund Bitzer und den anderen Tieren. Besonders gelungen fällt diesmal auch das etwas düstere Unterfangen aus, das auch kleinen Fans der kindgerechten „Shaun das Schaf“-Serie ein wenig Gruselatmosphäre zutraut.

Vishwendra Singh Talks “Khoriya”, Nepali Migrants, Documentary Realism and Life on the Margins of Delhi

Vishwendra Singh discusses “Khoriya”, Nepali migrants, documentary realism and finding authenticity through actors and real locations.

Vishwendra Singh’s “ Khoriya ” emerged from an attempt to document a community that, despite being highly visible within Indian cities, remains largely absent from mainstream representation. Centered on Nepali migrants living and working in Delhi, the film combines fiction with an intensely observational approach, following characters whose financial insecurity, precarious employment and outsider status leave them almost permanently in motion. Speaking with Asian Movie Pulse, Singh discussed the documentary origins of the project, the connection between the film’s bird-flu outbreak and COVID, its relentless tension, working with Nepali actors, and a production process that frequently allowed reality to determine what happened next.

Khoriya is screening at Busan International Film Festival

The origins of “Khoriya” go back to 2019, when Singh began making an informal documentary about Nepali migrants working in Indian cities. The subject had personal significance for him: he had grown up around Nepali people, had Nepali classmates, and his brother-in-law is Nepali. Yet he felt this substantial migrant community was rarely discussed within India. When COVID arrived in 2020, the documentary collapsed as Singh lost contact with several of his subjects. The stories, however, remained with him, eventually pushing him toward fiction as another way of exploring the same world.

COVID also entered the film indirectly. The avian-flu outbreak depicted in the story functions partly as a metaphor for the pandemic and for the experience of seeing livelihoods suddenly disappear. Singh points particularly toward Nepali workers occupying some of the least secure positions within poultry businesses, handling animals while facing the greatest physical risks and enjoying little protection. One of his protagonists has actually risen to become a poultry-farm manager, putting a Nepali character unusually in a position of authority, only to watch that status disappear when the outbreak destroys the business.

The constant tension running through “Khoriya” reflects this instability. Singh did not want the characters to appear as people with enough security to stop, evaluate their circumstances and calmly decide what to do next. Their lives simply do not provide that luxury. They are continually moving between jobs, places and problems, reacting to whatever circumstances impose upon them. Handheld camerawork, restless movement and the editing rhythm were all designed around this lack of stability, giving the sense that the characters are heading somewhere without ever knowing exactly where.

Check the review of the film

The film’s female character is approached very differently. Singh repeatedly films her from behind or avoids presenting her fully because the movie experiences her largely through the young man’s perspective. To him, she is almost a ghost from his past: the person who drew him toward the city but who never completely belongs to him. Singh was also conscious of stereotypes surrounding Nepali women in Delhi, particularly assumptions connecting them with salons, massage parlors and nighttime work. Rather than explaining exactly what she does, he deliberately preserves uncertainty around her life and keeps part of her identity beyond both the protagonist and the audience.

The resulting film is undeniably bleak, although Singh does not consider that a general statement about all Nepali migrants. He knows people who have overcome extremely difficult circumstances and built successful lives through their work. The bleakness instead reflects what he sees in the particular social environment occupied by these characters. As outsiders living within the urban underbelly, they remain especially vulnerable when something goes wrong: they can be blamed first, dismissed first and reminded immediately that they are considered not to belong.

Alcohol consequently appears less as casual recreation than as a way of temporarily escaping a reality over which the characters have little control. Singh clarified that another substance appearing in the story is not a recreational drug but steroids used in an attempt to pass army recruitment requirements. Alcoholism, however, is something he sees as a genuine social problem, particularly among people whose hopes remain alive while their surroundings continually undermine them. For such characters, drinking can become a way of briefly “checking out” from a claustrophobic existence.

One of the film’s most striking sequences, in which the young man’s head is forcibly shaved during army training, comes directly from Singh’s own experience. Coming from an army family and once expected to join the Indian Army himself, he remembers having his long hair shaved before recruitment. He also witnessed hair cutting being used to discipline and humiliate recruits who appeared insufficiently serious. In “Khoriya”, the humiliation acquires another layer because the other recruits laugh specifically when the Nepali character is subjected to it.

Remarkably, the scene itself was largely documentary. Singh filmed at a functioning training center using real army hopefuls and a real coach, without controlling their routine. The production had to arrive during their early-morning training and simply place the actors within the existing environment. Singh told the coach that the protagonist was a new recruit who had not been attending properly and asked what he would normally do. The coach replied that he would shave his head. Singh handed him a clipper and allowed the situation to unfold, even without discussing the decision with the actor beforehand. Afterward, the production took a day off to recalibrate, while the character’s newly shaved appearance ended up changing the rest of the film visually.

Casting presented one of the production’s greatest difficulties. Singh found that established casting networks in Mumbai and Delhi offered very limited access to Nepali and northeastern performers. Four months of street casting followed, particularly in Delhi neighborhoods with significant Nepali populations, but Singh initially encountered understandable suspicion from people who did not know him and had never considered themselves actors. Eventually, he travelled to Sikkim and contacted the National School of Drama’s local repertory. Two performers ultimately resigned from the repertory in order to join the film.

The younger brother was discovered in a considerably less conventional manner. At around 4:30 one morning, Singh was scrolling through Instagram when he encountered an absurd reel that made him laugh. He immediately messaged the young man about meeting for the film, received a response within a minute and quickly became convinced that he had found not simply an actor but the character himself. The performer playing the elder brother brought an even more direct connection to the material, having grown up around a family business involving a momo shop and poultry farm.

That authenticity meant Singh had to surrender some control. Since he was not from the community and did not fully speak the language, he refused to dictate dialogue and linguistic details he could not genuinely understand. Casting director Vinita Chamling Rai and the actors helped shape the language, tone and cultural specificity of individual scenes. A month and a half of workshops allowed them to repeatedly rewrite and perform dialogue until Singh could recognize its emotional rhythm almost musically, even when he could not understand every word literally.

Post-production proved almost as lengthy as the production itself. Because “Khoriya” was shot across separate periods, Singh initially edited the material himself after the first schedule. Following the second shoot, another editor reconstructed and expanded that version over approximately eight months. Selection for an NFDC film lab subsequently brought post-production funding and mentorship from experienced editors, while executive producer Ashim Ahluwalia helped further refine the film’s voice and structure. Altogether, Singh estimates that the editing process lasted roughly a year and a half.

Singh has already begun writing his next project, which moves into very different territory. The film will concern Indian soldiers during World War II, and he is currently taking meetings while preparing to pitch it. He also revealed that he discussed the project with Wim Wenders the previous year, although he is not yet ready to disclose further details.

“Khoriya”, however, remains closely connected to the filmmaker’s original documentary impulse. Its fiction repeatedly opens itself to real locations, real routines and people whose experiences are close to those of the characters. Rather than attempting to speak completely on behalf of a community outside his own, Singh built the production around collaboration, observation and occasionally relinquishing authority. The resulting film reflects characters who rarely control what happens to them, while the filmmaking itself repeatedly allowed an unpredictable reality to enter the frame.

article_text:
Nascida em um dos vários bairros segregados (as townships ) de Soweto, a fotojornalista Ruth Seopedi Motau (1968) foi a primeira fotógrafa negra a trabalhar como editora de fotografia na grande imprensa sul-africana. Motau começou sua vida profissional no final dos anos 1980 e início dos anos 1990, período de viu a libertação de Nelson Mandela e o fim da política separatista do apartheid. Ela conta que naquele momento “a África do Sul estava no centro das atenções. Nesse período, muitos fotojornalistas vieram à África do Sul e David Goldblatt os convidou para o MPW. James Naftali veio e me lembro que também esteve aqui o Sebastião Salgado, que é o meu fotógrafo favorito.”

Em conversa com a pesquisadora e curadora Ana Paula Vitorio, Motau fala do início da sua carreira, do seu pioneirismo nas redações da grande imprensa como mulher fotógrafa negra e da importância de abrir este espaço dentro dos jornais: “Normalmente o que eu fazia era recrutar mulheres fotógrafas, mas mulheres negras ainda não havia muitas. Acho que um dos motivos era também a dificuldade da nossa cultura em reconhecer fotógrafos e artistas. Nossos pais diziam ‘o que você vai fazer da vida? Como vai colocar pão na mesa?’ Não havia muito suporte. Foi por isso que eu criei um programa de mentoria.”

Dra. Ruth, como começou a sua relação com a fotografia?

Ruth Motau: Eu nunca falo sobre isso, mas minha paixão era a música. Eu queria estudar música. Mas se naquele período [apartheid] você fosse negra e das townships era muito difícil. Então eu acabei na fotografia por acidente e me apaixonei por ela.

Como foi esse acidente?

RM: Eu visitei uma fundação com uma colega do ensino médio que me convidou para ir até lá. Ela disse que era um espaço de arte e que talvez eu pudesse encontrar algo que me interessasse lá. Mas quando você ainda está nessa busca, você nem sabe ao certo o que procura nem o que quer fazer. Um tempo depois e comecei a frequentar o Alexander Arts Centre , que era onde o Victor Matom dava aulas naquela época. Eu fiquei por lá por alguns meses, mas então ouvi falar sobre o que o David Goldblatt estava fazendo no Market Theatre . O Alexander ficava longe da minha casa. Para ir até lá eu precisava pegar dois taxis, mas para ir ao Market Theatre eu só precisaria de um – e às vezes eu não tinha dinheiro algum. Então eu comecei a fazer o Market Photo Workshop (MPW). Acabei ficando lá por três anos.

Naquela época eu não tinha certeza se eu teria um futuro como fotógrafa. Certa vez, no início dos anos 1990, um jornal abriu uma chamada para estágio. Meus colegas do MPW se candidataram e um deles foi contratado. Isso despertou meu interesse, uns anos depois eu comecei a ver as fotos dele no jornal e pensei “eu também quero estar lá”. Mas eu não tinha certeza se eu era capaz, sabe? Então me lembro que um dia eu estava no MPW e um outro colega que era branco contou que tinha se inscrito para preencher uma dessas vagas, mas que tinha sido recusado porque o jornal estava procurando por pessoas negras. Mesmo assim, eu não me candidatei. Então eu recebi uma ligação do Kevin Carter pedindo que eu levasse meu portfólio porque ele queria dar uma olhada. Eu fui até lá numa sexta ou sábado e no domingo ele me ligou dizendo “você começa na segunda”. Foi assim que aconteceu.

Esse foi o seu primeiro jornal? O Weekly Mail ?

RM: Sim, foi o início da minha carreira e foi quando eu comecei a entender o que é fotografia. Eu digo isso porque naquela época o Weekly Mail era publicado junto com o The Guardian , de Londres. Eu tinha acesso ao The Guardian e observava como eles publicavam as coisas. Eles faziam um excelente trabalho. O Weekly Mail publicava também notícias internacionais e isso para mim era muito emocionante.

A senhora pode me contar um pouco mais sobre como foi seu tempo aluna no Market Photo Workshop ?

RM: Naquela época David Goldblatt ainda estava dando aulas. Eu lembro de estar em algumas turmas em que ele foi professor. Era o começo nos anos 1990, a África do Sul estava no centro das atenções. Mandela tinha sido libertado, o apartheid estava chegando ao fim. As coisas estavam começando a tomar forma. Nesse período, muitos fotojornalistas vieram à África do Sul e David Goldblatt os convidou para o MPW. James Naftali veio e me lembro que também esteve aqui o Sebastião Salgado, que é o meu fotógrafo favorito. Todo mundo que nós admirávamos e que tinha trabalhos que nos inspiravam esteve aqui, deu aulas e palestras para nós. Eles nos motivaram. Essa foi a melhor época das nossas vidas.

A senhora começou no jornal ainda na década de 1990. O que significava para uma mulher negra ser fotojornalista em um veículo sul-africano naquele período?

RM: No início, quando eu comecei no jornal, eu só queria ver como as coisas eram porque eu ainda não conhecia bem como tudo funcionava. Uma vez que você está contratada, eles te enviam para fazer uma história em Soweto sobre uma escola, por exemplo, você vai faz a história e volta. Na maioria das vezes, eles só iriam publicar uma fotografia e talvez nenhuma. Me incomodava muito o fato de as coberturas, especialmente quando se tratava de histórias sobre pessoas negras, não mostravam as coisas como elas realmente eram. Principalmente no que diz respeito às fotografias. Isso porque o jornal impresso é sobre espaço, venda de espaço, de publicidade para gerar lucro. Mas digamos que você vai fazer uma matéria sobre um programa de alimentação. Para mim, há a fotografia das pessoas que se beneficiam daquele programa, há a fotografia da comida sendo preparada na cozinha etc. É mais do que uma única imagem fotográfica. Tem a questão da origem desse alimento, a horta de onde ele vem, o preparo na cozinha, as crianças recebendo a comida e depois comendo. Mas muitas vezes eles [os editores] dizem que o que você tem que fazer é apenas uma fotografia, a da pessoa que oferece aquele programa de alimentação. Não é isso! As fotografias que realmente importam acabam ficando de lado. Foi aí que comecei a pensar: sei contar histórias melhor que isso. Então disse a mim mesma: preciso documentar nossas vidas, nossas histórias, porque se eu não contar as histórias da maneira que conheço, elas sempre serão distorcidas. Foi então que comecei a fazer esse tipo de trabalho, a tomar a iniciativa independente do que fosse. E isso durante aquela época de violência [apartheid]. Eu me lembro de contar ao Kevin, meu chefe, que eu era da township , que eu era diretamente afetada por toda aquela violência. Eu queria fazer algo diferente, criar histórias que nos fizessem sentir vivos, histórias que diriam que estávamos lá, que estivemos lá. Então comecei a criar histórias, reportagens especiais. Eu comecei a entender porque estava fazendo fotografia, era porque eu queria contar a minha própria história.

O que a senhora costumava cobrir? Quais os principais temas e assuntos?

RM: Qualquer coisa. Eu cobria muitas igrejas porque havia muitas e diferentes igrejas. Era apenas o cotidiano das pessoas negras vivendo, entende? Às vezes, eu simplesmente carregava minha câmera e fotografava as pessoas ali onde elas estivessem. Eu passava por uma mulher sentada na porta ouvindo rádio e a fotografava. Eu gostava de simplesmente fotografar a vida cotidiana. Estava só tentando contar a nossa história. Porque não era tudo sempre sobre violência e morte. Havia pessoas, a vida acontecia. A mulher dessa foto estava lá sentada, vivendo e isso é lindo, entende? Eu tenho muitas fotografias como essa, sobre o que estava acontecendo nas nossas vidas. Porque a vida seguia, nós fazíamos coisas, estávamos vivos. Isso era o que eu documentava, a vida. Muitas vezes você olha o jornal, para a forma como eles nos representam e sabe que não é a verdade. E então eu disse a mim mesma: a única maneira de mostrar a verdade é lutando por ela, é fazendo o real trabalho que precisa ser feito.

A senhora se torna editora em um jornal logo após o fim institucional do apartheid. Como foi esse período e sua trajetória na edição de fotojornalismo?

RM: Eu nunca me vi como uma editora, eu me via como uma fotógrafa. Naquela época, eu costumava editar o trabalho de muitas pessoas, mas eu também saia às ruas e fotografava. Então eu não estava apenas lá na redação, tomando decisões lá de dentro. Eu também estava criando e trazendo trabalho. Apenas muitos anos depois de me aposentar foi que olhei para trás e entendi que o que eu fazia era de fato edição. Eu trabalhei com muitas pessoas de todo o país. Mas foi anos depois que me dei conta da enorme responsabilidade que eu tinha na luta por fazer com que a representação fotográfica no jornal fosse a melhor possível. Mas, às vezes, essa decisão não cabia apenas a mim. Eu tinha um chefe e às vezes ele dizia “eu quero isso e não aquilo”. A gente discutia, brigava. Às vezes eu ganhava, mas às vezes eu perdia. Só que há um momento em que você chega ao seu limite, quer fazer outras coisas. Depois de nove anos eu saí do jornal e comecei a atuar como freelancer. Eu comecei a fazer as coisas que amava novamente. Trabalhei com investimento social e viajava pelo país fazendo isso.

Um tempo depois eu fui recrutada para ser editora de fotografia no maior jornal diário das townships , o Sowetan . Eu cresci lendo o Sowetan , então eu cheguei lá e me deparei com todos aqueles nomes que eu havia lido por anos, foi muito excitante. Trabalhei lá por quatro anos e depois eu fui para o City Press , também como editora de fotografia. Lá eu fiquei por dois anos. Eu saí em um período em que as redes sociais estavam surgindo e a gente já podia sentir o impresso enfrentando problemas.

Na sua opinião, por que demorou tanto tempo para que jornais importantes contratassem mulheres negras como editoras?

Ruth: Não havia muitas mulheres negras nos jornais. Ainda hoje há poucas. Na minha época, o The Mailing Garden [formalmente, o Weekly Mail ] era o único. Quando eu saí de lá eu ainda era a única. Normalmente o que eu fazia era recrutar mulheres fotógrafas, mas mulheres negras ainda não havia muitas. Acho que um dos motivos era também a dificuldade da nossa cultura em reconhecer fotógrafos e artistas. Nossos pais diziam “o que você vai fazer da vida? Como vai colocar pão na mesa?” Não havia muito suporte. Foi por isso que eu criei um programa de mentoria. Eu comecei a atuar como mentora de mulheres negras das townships e das áreas rurais e dizia a elas, vocês podem fazer isso! Vocês podem publicar livros, trabalhar em jornais, fazer o que quiserem. Da mesma forma que os homens, vocês também podem fazer isso. Eu costumava ligar para jovens fotógrafas e as convidava para trabalhar comigo por três meses. Fiz isso por muitos anos em todos os jornais em que atuei. Lembro que eu contratei, por exemplo, Makgotso Gulube como fotógrafa no Sowetan . Eu poderia ter contratado homens brilhantes, mas a convidei. Para mim era sobre trazer mulheres negras para dentro.

Hoje a senhora tem um programa próprio de mentoria. Como ele funciona especificamente?

RM: Eu comecei durante a pandemia. No programa eu não ensino desde o básico, o que eu faço é ajudá-las a desenvolver as histórias que elas querem contar. Auxilio em como abordar essas histórias, como documentá-las. Às vezes as pessoas dizem: Ruth, eu quero desenvolver tal projeto, mas não sei como. Eu digo a elas: apenas continue fotografando. Não pare de fotografar e fotografar. Em algum momento você vai sentir no seu espirito: é isso, agora tenho fotografias o bastante. Pode ser que você consiga isso em um dia, mas pode ser que seja preciso mais tempo. Acho que é parecido com escrever ou com ouvir música. Às vezes a gente escuta uma música e ela simplesmente não faz sentido, pode ser que você sequer entenda a letra. Mas 20 anos depois, você escuta novamente e diz “ah então era sobre isso!”. Acho que é o mesmo com a arte.

A senhora continua fotografando?

RM: Sim, mas não tanto. Hoje eu escolho o que fazer. Eu posso deixar a fotografia de lado, ficar entediada, fazer outras coisas por um tempo, mas eu sempre volto para a fotografia, ela é meu primeiro amor. É algo que eu posso fazer de olhos fechados, a qualquer hora e em qualquer lugar, então eu sempre volto para a fotografia.

E o que a senhora escolhe hoje?

RM: Estou trabalhando em um projeto chamado Black Beauty [Beleza Negra] que é sobre corpos negros. Eu não acredito que exista nada que seja feito. Tudo é belo por ser único. Mas nesse trabalho eu busco por figuras e posturas corporais específicas, é um projeto de retratos. O mundo nos fez acreditar que somos inferiores por causa da cor da nossa pele, do formato do nosso corpo. Mas somos lindas e na verdade eles querem ser como nós. Nós também queremos ser como eles por causa da mentira que nos contaram dizendo a nós que somos feias. Então esse projeto é sobre dizer às pessoas negras: seu corpo é lindo, você é linda. ///

article_text:
K-pop star Rosé will perform at LACMA’s upcoming Art+Film Gala on November 7.

The Blackpink vocalist joins the museum’s 15th annual fundraiser, which will honor Latvian American artist Vija Celmins, long celebrated for her meticulous renderings of the natural world, and Denis Villeneuve, the director behind cerebral sci-fi hits Dune and Arrival . The event is presented again by Gucci, with actor Leonardo DiCaprio and LACMA trustee Eva Chow returning as co-chairs.

“The LACMA Art+Film Gala celebrates creative icons and the connections between all forms of creativity, all around the world,” said Chow in a statement. “As a global pop superstar, Rosé will amplify the spirit of the evening with her incomparable talent and style.”

As its name suggests, the Art+Film Gala each year honors a visual artist and a filmmaker, and has become a fixture of Los Angeles’s art calendar since its first edition in 2011, which was dedicated to John Baldessari and Clint Eastwood. The 2025 gala raised $6.5 million, a figure slightly higher than the $6.4 million it brought in the previous year.

Rosé follows a roster of high-profile musical guests that includes Doja Cat in 2025, Annie Lennox in 2017, and Charli XCX, who brought out Troye Sivan as a surprise guest for her 2024 performance. Rosé’s appearance at the Art+Film Gala is hardly a first: she attended in both 2022 and 2023. Beyond Blackpink’s stratospheric success, her debut solo studio album, rosie , has surpassed 10 billion streams, buoyed by “APT.” That hit collaboration with Bruno Mars earned her three Grammy nominations.

For those who can afford a ticket, which start at $10,000, say hello to the number one girl .

article_text:
A proposed Bangladeshi soccer league and an Indonesian film joint venture sit at the center of Goldfinch International’s move into Bangladesh and Indonesia.

The company is the emerging-markets division of London-based entertainment financier and producer Goldfinch.

In both countries, Goldfinch International is following the approach it took in the Gulf with Fablemill, building ties with governments and institutions.

Its Bangladesh partner is 1CS Holdings Limited, headed by Nazir Alam, which is originating and steering the local projects. The two companies have joined forces with Fablemill and Germany’s Akani Group to create the Bangladesh Strategic Partnership (BSP), a consortium set up to draw foreign investment, institutional ties and skills training into the country’s sports and creative sectors.

Earlier this month, BSP and the Bangladesh Football Federation (BFF) signed an MoU to look into building the proposed Bangladesh Super League. The competition would mix existing clubs with regional franchises and bring in professional governance alongside international commercial know-how and investment. The consortium plans to approach British and European clubs, family offices, specialist investors and members of the Bangladeshi diaspora. Beyond the league, it is also eyeing soccer facilities, academies, athlete rehab, creative skills training and sports employment.

“Bangladesh has extraordinary potential in sport, technology and the creative economy, particularly through the talent and aspirations of Generation Z,” said Alam, who is executive chairman of BSP. “Our partnership aims to connect that potential with British and European expertise, international investors and credible commercial opportunities. The MoU with the Bangladesh Football Federation is an important first step toward building a wider ecosystem of investment, skills, employment and international collaboration.”

BSP has also opened conversations with the Bangladesh Olympic Association, the ICT Division, Startup Bangladesh and the Ministry of Youth and Sports about possible sports infrastructure and institutional cooperation. Separately, the group is weighing a National Creative Economy Partnership that would cover international production, creative infrastructure, IP and technology, as well as openings for the country’s younger generation.

In Indonesia, Goldfinch has entered a joint venture opportunity partnership with Jakarta creative company Rangkai. The deal follows the MoU that Goldfinch signed with Rangkai and the Jakarta Film Commission at the Cannes Film Festival in May.

The venture pairs Rangkai’s standing in Indonesia’s filmmaking community, its local distribution track record and its government and industry connections with Goldfinch’s global sales network, production financing and deal-structuring expertise. It will be active in community building, distribution, global sales, production and advisory work, with the goal of putting Indonesian talent and stories in front of overseas buyers, partners and investors.

Rangkai CEO Redemptus Rangga Raditya said the company has spent five years building ties with Indonesian filmmakers, government and audiences. “In Goldfinch we have a partner that brings the international reach and financing experience to take Indonesian stories to the world, and we are proud to be building this together as equals,” he said.

The Gulf template came from a strategic tie-up that Goldfinch International launched at Cannes this year with Fablemill, a Gulf-based creative industries advisory led by Eman Alsabah. Also backing the wider platform are a production debt fund for emerging markets that launched in 2025 and is set to start deploying capital in early 2027, and Vault 47, a Singapore branded entertainment studio formed in late 2025 with Virtue, with guidance from Justin Deimen, David Webster and Lesley John. Goldfinch International said it is in talks with partners in several more Global South territories.

“Bangladesh and Indonesia are two of the youngest and largest markets in the world, and in 1CS Holdings and Rangkai we have partners who sit inside government and inside the creative community at the same time,” said Phil McKenzie, co-founder and COO of Goldfinch. “Our role is to bring the capital, structure and international relationships that turn that access into leagues, studios and skilled jobs. With Fablemill in the Gulf, Vault 47 in Singapore and the Commonwealth Creative Industries Alliance now reaching 56 nations, Goldfinch International is quickly becoming a genuine platform for the Global South.”

In November, the Goldfinch team will travel to the Commonwealth Heads of Government Meeting in Antigua and Barbuda to promote the Commonwealth Creative Industries Alliance, and will unveil more development programs there. Goldfinch launched the alliance this year with the Commonwealth Foundation and the Commonwealth Businesswomen’s Network as an events, advisory and research outfit for creative industries across all 56 Commonwealth nations.

article_text:
Unionized staff across all four branches of the Victoria & Albert Museum in London announced their intention to strike on October 29 and 30, citing stalled negotiations and allegations of “Amazon-style” working conditions at the newly opened V&A East Storehouse.

The announcement follows two planned strikes in September at three V&A museums by workers represented by Prospect Union’s heritage division and the Public and Commercial Services Union (PCS). The V&A preemptively closed the three locations in response to the strike threat, a move it described in a statement at the time as a “difficult decision.”

Staff at the V&A East Storehouse, a publicly accessible museum storage facility in East London, had voted unanimously in July to strike, claiming they are denied enough time to use the bathroom or drink water. According to a statement from Prospect, the museum has not granted the union’s “extremely reasonable request” for two paid breaks per day.

“Prospect members are dedicated to their jobs, and it is these dedicated staff who make the museum the world-class attraction it is,” said Prospect Union’s general secretary, Mike Clancy, in a press statement. Clancy also claimed that V&A Director Tristram Hunt had refused to negotiate with the unions, which he said “shows the level of disdain in which he holds his staff.”

The V&A has denied the union’s allegations about working conditions at the Storehouse. A museum spokesperson told ARTnews following the strike vote that “all our staff have access to water and toilet facilities and regular breaks while at work,” noting that neither staff nor visitors are allowed to bring food or drinks near the collection.

Among other demands, the V&A unions have called on the museum to become a Real London Living Wage-accredited employer, which would guarantee all staff an hourly wage matching London’s cost of living, currently estimated at £14.80 (about $20). The unions have also demanded a minimum 4% pay bump for workers earning above the living wage, time and a half for work on bank holidays, and measures across all V&A sites to shade outdoor spaces when temperatures are forecast at 30°C (86°F) or higher, along with better cooling in back-of-house areas.

The V&A told ARTnews that it has been negotiating in good faith with the unions since February and that its latest pay offer meets the original demands, including a 4.18 percent average pay increase, a 6.9 percent pay increase for the lowest-paid employees, also claiming to Hyperallergic that “all our staff are already paid at least the London Living Wage – and work is underway reviewing accreditation.” The spokesperson said that the museum had also agreed to 50% pay bump for bank holidays.

PCS, however, said in a public statement Tuesday that the V&A has not settled the dispute. According to the union, while the 6.9 percent pay bump for the lowest-paid staff was offered, most employees have only been offered a 3.25 percent base increase, and that the organization is “refusing to become London Living Wage accredited.” PCS claims that “several” Storehouse employees have fainted due to the ban on carrying even sealed water bottles into the storage area, and that the facilities’ water fountains are regularly out of order.

Furthermore, the statement claimed, “During private events at Storehouse, food and drink have been served in the collections hall,” adding that “Our members have even found empty beer bottles in this area the day after an event.”

“Staff deserve fair pay, safe working conditions and respect,” said PCS general secretary Fran Heathcote in the statement. “We urge the V&A to make meaningful progress and resolve this dispute.”

article_text:
Two-time Oscar nominee Emily Watson has joined the Oscar-qualified short film “The Drive” as executive producer, lending her support to husband-and-wife filmmaking team David Arrow and Amber Paul as the film enters awards season.

Set on a warm November afternoon in the early 1960s, “The Drive” is inspired by a little-known episode that unfolded on the day President John F. Kennedy was assassinated.

The film follows Liz (Paul) during a routine school carpool when news of the assassination breaks, transforming an ordinary journey into a drive she will never forget. Rather than revisit the historic event itself, “The Drive” looks at its immediate human impact through the intimate perspective of a mother suddenly confronted with a nation-changing tragedy.

Watson, who has been friends with Arrow for many years, says she was drawn to the film’s understated approach to a moment embedded in the public consciousness.

“’The Drive’ delivers a fresh insight into a moment that is universally known, with utter clarity,” she said. “Beautifully shot and acted, being both emotionally truthful and understated, the brief but deeply touching story is rendered vividly with a texture that is absolutely of its time; with the lightest of touches we are slowly made aware that we are inside a very intimate and personal private detail of an historic world-shattering event seared in the public imagination.”

Following screenings at more than 40 film festivals and multiple awards, the film is now qualified for consideration for the 99th Academy Awards.

“As familiar as I am with the overall events that took place, I was stunned that I didn’t know this small but significant piece of history, a very personal and compelling footnote to one of the most consequential chapters in the chronicle of the 20th century,” said Arrow.

Produced through 4 A Films, “The Drive” continues the creative partnership between Arrow and Paul. Arrow’s screen credits include “Igby Goes Down,” “Hostage,” “Broad City,” NBC’s “The Hunting Party” and AMC’s “Turn.” Paul is an award-winning actress whose credits include “The Woman From Hamburg,” “That’s My Boy,” “Nurse Jackie” and “Music for a Sushi Restaurant” opposite Harry Styles.

Watson received Oscar nominations for “Breaking the Waves” and “Hilary and Jackie.” Her most recent credits include her Berlin International Film Festival Silver Bear performance in “Small Things Like These,” opposite Cillian Murphy, and in Chloé Zhao’s “Hamnet.”

article_text:
Abramorama has acquired North American theatrical distribution rights to John David Coles documentary The Choice and set a Jan 15 release date at the Quad in NYC followed by a national rollout.

Winner of the Brizzolara Family Foundation Award for Films of Conflict & Resolution at the 2026 Hamptons International Film Festival, The Choice is eligible for an Academy Award for Best Feature Documentary. See trailer below.

A Talking Wall/Gigantic Pictures film produced by Coles, Jason Orans, Pamela Ryan and Tamar Yoffe, the doc interweaves the stories of three women across generations, each marked by war, captivity, and loss: the late Edith “Edie” Eger, renowned psychologist, Holocaust survivor and author of 2017 bestseller The Choice: Embrace the Possible ; Iris Haim, an Israeli mother whose son Yotam was taken hostage during the October 7 attacks; and Sapir Cohen, who survived 55 days as a hostage in Gaza. The doc moves between past and present with archival footage, interviews, public appearances, audio recordings and personal writings.

Related Stories

Abramorama Acquires 'One More Time' About New York Theater Trio Tackling Beckett's 'Endgame'; Scorsese Exec-Produces; Watch Trailer

Eger passed away last May at 98. The central pillar of her life and work is that while we cannot change what has happened to us, we can choose how we live now. Having survived Auschwitz, Eger devoted her life to helping Vietnam veterans and others confront trauma, guilt and grief.

Watch on Deadline

“Dr. Edith Eger taught millions of readers through her book that even in the face of unthinkable suffering, we keep the freedom to decide who we become,” said Karol Martesko-Fenster, CEO of AB2 Media Group and Abramorama. “John David Coles has carried that message into the present with extraordinary grace and urgency. At a time when so many people are carrying grief, this film offers a way forward.”

Nonprofit Theorem will host a Global Virtual Watch Event on Kinema Nov. 19 with a live conversation with Coles and Eger’s daughter, clinical psychologist Marianne Engle.

“I set out to make a film about Edie Eger’s legacy and discovered that her legacy was still being written,” said Coles. “Trauma can echo across generations, but so can resilience, and so can hope. My wish is that audiences leave the theater knowing that even when the worst has already happened, we still have a say in how we carry it.”

article_text:
Steven Soderbergh is stepping in to help complete “The Batman Part II” while director Matt Reeves is on hiatus dealing with a personal matter, Variety has confirmed.

“As Matt Reeves continues to attend to an ongoing family matter, Steven Soderbergh, as an admirer of Matt’s work, approached Matt and will step in, with the full support of DC Studios, to help the writer-director complete the final weeks of principal photography on ‘The Batman Part 2,'” a studio rep said in a statement. “Matt and Steven will work closely together with the actors and crew to fulfill Matt’s vision of the film.”

Related Stories

Ju Ji-hoon, Choo Young-woo Return for Netflix’s ‘The Trauma Code: Heroes on Call’ Seasons 2 and 3

Netflix Content Chief Bela Bajaria on Overseeing Global Storytelling: 'My Super Power Is I Hire Really Great People and I Let Them Do Their Job'

Soderbergh said in his own statement, “I thought Matt Reeves’ work on ‘The Batman’ was stunning; it was intentional, specific and rigorously coherent. The goal here is to work with Matt and his team to generate footage that will integrate seamlessly with what’s already been shot so Matt can properly finish his film.”

Reeves clarified on X that he will still be working on the production, just not on the set while principal photography wraps up.

Just to be clear, I am not leaving The Batman Part II. I am profoundly grateful to Steven for coming to my aid during this challenging time to help me finish principal photography. Thank you to all for your concern and well wishes. 🦇 — Matt Reeves (@mattreevesLA) October 15, 2026

Warner Bros. and DC Studios announced “The Batman Part II” production pause in early October, stating that Reeves temporarily stepped away from the project to handle a “family matter.”

“Production on ‘The Batman Part II’ has been temporarily paused while Matt Reeves focuses on a family matter,” a rep said in a statement at the time. “Matt has the full support of DC Studios and we look forward to continuing the journey soon.”

Soderbergh is the Oscar-winning director best known for films “Traffic,” “Erin Brockovich,” “Sex, Lies, and Videotape and “Ocean’s Eleven.” His most recent releases include “The Christophers,” “Black Bag,” “Presence” and “John Lennon: The Last Interview.”

The highly anticipated “Batman” sequel has experienced several delays since it was announced at CinemaCon 2022. The original release date was set for Oct. 2, 2026, before Warner Bros. delayed it to Oct. 1, 2027. In June, the film was pushed again to February 2028. Reeves’ first “Batman” was released in March 2022.

Robert Pattinson returns as the Caped Crusader in “The Batman Part II.” Other cast members include Scarlett Johansson, Colin Farrell, Sebastian Stan, Andy Serkis and Jeffrey Wright.

editorial_blocks_json: [{"type": "paragraph", "text": "AT&T Untold Stories Award是同类中全球规模最大的电影奖项。每年有数百名电影人申请角逐这一奖项，其中包括120万美元的资金支持，以及帮助他们完成电影创作的导师网络与资源扶持。这些候选人经过筛选进入最后5强，他们将有机会在翠贝卡电影节上，在座无虚席的观众和评委团面前进行电影路演。赢得他们的青睐，你就有机会将自己的电影愿景变为现实。", "links": [{"text": "film", "url": "https://www.indiewire.com/t/film/"}], "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "大卫·福琼深知这个奖项的分量。这位2023年AT&T Untold Stories Award得主利用这笔资助拍摄了他的2024年长片《Color Book》，该片目前正在Netflix上流媒体播放。", "translated": true}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://www.indiewire.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/RP_B2706.jpg?w=300&h=168&crop=1", "alt": "阿拉什·阿什蒂亚尼、佩加·阿汉加拉尼和布伦特·兰格于2026年10月19日在加利福尼亚州洛杉矶的Lumen出席IndieWire艺术纪录片2026峰会。", "caption": "", "credit": "IndieWire", "translated": true}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://www.indiewire.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/202605733_1_RWD_1920.jpg?w=300&h=168&crop=1", "alt": "谁杀了亚歷克斯·奥德？", "caption": "", "credit": "IndieWire", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "这部电影讲述了一位单亲父亲抚养患有唐氏综合症的儿子并带他去观看第一场棒球比赛的故事，这正是该项目旨在支持的那类作品。它讲述了一个关于黑人单亲育儿的细腻故事，而我们在银幕上很少见到这样的视角，这一切都通过一位独具天赋的电影人的声音呈现出来。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "在由AT&T呈现的IndieWire“电影制作未来峰会”的一场对话中，福琼阐述了他如何看待这个最终改变了他命运的机会。", "links": [{"text": "Future of Filmmaking", "url": "https://www.indiewire.com/t/future-of-filmmaking/"}], "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "“我想说是准备，”福琼在被问及给未来参赛者的建议时说道。“你无法控制自己是赢是输，但你可以控制自己如何准备。我知道自己会紧张得要死，但即便在紧张状态下，我也要确保自己能够正确路演，以一种能给自己带来最大获胜机会的方式展现自己。我只想成为房间里准备得最充分的人。”", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "为了确保在面对人群路演时没有任何事物能动摇自己，这种准备甚至将他的身体推向了极限。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "“我跳进淋浴间，把水温调到你能调到的最冰冷的档位。然后我跳进去说：‘现在开始你的路演，’”他笑着说。“我不得不在体温过低的情况下路演！因为如果你在被锁喉的情况下都无法路演，又怎么能在舞台上路演呢？”", "translated": true}, {"type": "image", "url": "https://img.connatix.com/ad08f596-5956-400f-a9ed-471076d7f19f/1_th.jpg", "alt": "莉莲·梅雷尔 - 电影制作未来", "caption": "", "credit": "IndieWire", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "当然，福琼的方法并不是唯一行之有效的方法。这次展示还播放了2024年比赛得主莉莲·T·梅雷尔的视频讯息，她利用奖金拍摄了她的长片处女作《Honeyjooon》。她回忆了自己路演电影的过程，以及当她最终能够向观众展示成品时所获得的认可。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "“在那天路演时，我知道如果我能让观众笑、让观众哭、引发情感共鸣，并让他们感受到属于我声音的作者电影喜剧风格，那么我就会赢。而我做到了！”梅雷尔说道，并补充说该片随后在50多个电影节上放映。“身处观众席中，听到人们一起欢笑、一起感动……那真是一种触电般的体验。它给了我燃料，让我明白这部电影必须在院线上映。”", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "在上方视频中观看与福琼的完整对话。", "translated": true}, {"type": "paragraph", "text": "IndieWire 2026年电影制作未来峰会由AT&T Untold Stories呈现，这是AT&T与翠贝卡电影节之间具有影响力的多年期合作项目，向渴望将电影搬上大银幕的下一代电影人提供120万美元奖金、导师指导和全方位支持。欲了解更多信息，请访问此处。", "links": [{"text": "visit here", "url": "https://tribecafilm.com/attuntoldstories"}], "translated": true}]

article_text:
The AT&T Untold Stories Award is the world’s largest filmmaking award of its kind. Each year, hundreds of filmmakers apply to be considered for a prize that includes $1.2 million and a network of mentorship and support to help them make a film . Those candidates are narrowed down to five finalists who get a chance to pitch their film in front of a packed audience and a panel of judges at the Tribeca Festival. Win them over, and you might get a chance to bring your cinematic vision to life.

David Fortune knows just how impactful the prize can be. The filmmaker, who won the 2023 AT&T Untold Stories Award, used the grant to make his 2024 feature “Color Book,” which is now streaming on Netflix.

The film, which tells the story of a single father raising a son with Down syndrome who takes him to his first baseball game, is exactly the kind of project that the program exists to support. It tells a nuanced story about Black single parenthood that we had seldom seen on screen, all filtered through the voice of one distinctly talented filmmaker.

During a conversation at IndieWire’s Future of Filmmaking Summit, presented by AT&T, Fortune explained how he approached an opportunity that turned out to be life-changing.

“I would say preparation,” Fortune said when asked to give advice to future contestants. “You can’t control if you win or lose, but you can control how you prepare. I knew I was gonna be nervous as hell, but even in my nervousness I wanted to make sure I was able to pitch correctly and present myself in a way that gave me my best chance to win. I just wanted to be the most prepared person in the room.”

That preparation saw him pushing his body to his limits to ensure that nothing would shake him when it was time to pitch in front of a crowd.

“I jumped in the shower, and I put it on the most ice cold level you could put it in. And I jumped in and said ‘Say your pitch now,’ he said with a laugh. “I had to pitch with hypothermia! Because if you can’t pitch in a chokehold, how are you going to pitch on stage?”

Of course, Fortune’s process is not the only approach that can work. The presentation also featured a video message from Lilian T. Mehrel, who won the 2024 competition and used the prize money to make her feature debut “Honeyjooon.” She recalled her own process of pitching her film, and the validation that she received when she was finally able to show the finished product to audiences.

“That day that I pitched, I knew if I could make audiences laugh and cry and feel emotional and get a sense of the auteur cinematic comedy stamp that is my voice, then I would win. And I did!” Mehrel said, adding that the film went on to play over 50 festivals. “Being in the audience, hearing people laugh and get emotional together… it was just this electric experience. It gave me the fuel to know that this film needs to be released in theaters.”

IndieWire Future of Filmmaking 2026 Summit is presented by AT&T Untold Stories, an impactful multi-year collaboration between AT&T and Tribeca Festival that awards $1.2 million dollars, mentorship, and comprehensive support to the next generation of filmmakers looking to bring their films to the big screen.
